title: Burst resonance scheduler scrapbook
content:
Context: personal breadcrumb-style log while investigating a recurring dedicated-capacity instability observed in the west-us cluster. Symptoms: brief periods (30s-3m) of high eviction/queue growth followed by catch-up waves; observed a repeating ‘burst then quiet’ pattern across several dedicated pools. Hypothesis evolving: scheduling/ramping heuristic + eviction window misalignment -> cascading restarts and over-provisioning oscillation. Also possible interaction with new eviction grace change rolled in Oct (controller v2).

Chronological notes / probes

2024-11-05 09:12 - first handoff
- User report: latency spikes for hosted customers on dedicated pools, concurrent gen requests increase 10x for short window.
- Quick check: dashboard shows token-rate spike + GPU utilization drop to 0 for ~45s on 3 nodes.

Commands I ran (quick, from laptop via bastion):
- kubectl -n serving get pods -l pool=dedicated-westus -o wide
  Output: many pods in RUNNING, a handful in Terminating during spike

- kubectl -n serving describe pod <pod-id> | egrep -i "(oom|evict|preempt|terminated)"
  Snippet: "Container runtime terminating container: preemption-triggered eviction: node reclaim" (saw twice)

- k get hpa -n serving
  HPA shows scaleTarget: serving-deployment-xyz, minReplicas: 2, maxReplicas: 10

- curl http://metrics.internal:9090/metrics | grep pool_warm_duration_seconds
  metric shows many short-lived warm durations at ~12-18s for same pool

- kubectl logs controller-manager -n kube-system | tail -n 200 | grep "scaleDown" -i
  Found: controller: scaleDown in-flight; reason: UtilizationBelowThreshold -> triggered ephemeral drain

Observed pattern:
- Ramp triggers (scaleUp) quickly when queue backs up; autoscaler requests nodes/GPUs.
- Node provisioning takes ~30s to start VM + 20s to attach GPU + extra 10s for runtime.
- Meanwhile scheduler evicts lower-priority pods to make room -> creates churn. When new nodes come, scheduler prefers moving pods back -> additional migrations.
- Once new capacity stabilizes, OOM-like cleanup from leftover init containers causes brief termination signals -> more reschedules.
- After ~2 minutes system re-converges.

Experiment 1 (11/06 14:00): slowed down autoscaler by adjusting cooldown to 90s on test pool
- changed ConfigMap: autoscaler.cooldownSeconds = "90"
- Result: peak queue lengths stayed higher but oscillation frequency dropped. Latency tail improved slightly, but cold-start latency for new requests increased.
- Logs: fewer scaleDown/scaleUp cycles seen.

Experiment 2 (11/07 02:30): disabled preemptive eviction for a canary pool
- kubectl patch nodepool dedicated-westus-canary -p '{"spec":{"evictionPolicy":"none"}}'
- Result: fewer terminations but some nodes hit memory pressure and pod OOMKilled; less churn but higher risk of noisy neighbor affecting throughput.

Error snippets collected:
- "PodEvicted: insufficient gpu" (seen when scheduler moved workloads)
- "kubelet: container runtime is shutting down" (timing aligned with node bump)
- "gpus.attacher: timeout attaching device 15s" (rare) - possibly NVML attach lag on older hosts

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Autoscaler cooldown too short + immediate scaleDown heuristic => thrash. When scaleDown triggers during residual ramp activity, the controller removes capacity that other autoscalers expect to remain.
2) Scheduling scores skewed by recent pod footprints: pods with large KV caches prefer warmed nodes; scheduler moves them aggressively when capacity returns, causing heavy data movement.
3) Preemptive eviction policy interacts poorly with VM provisioning timing; eviction runs too eagerly when temporary GC spikes occur.
4) GPU attach latency for some instance types causes scheduling delays and leads controller to think attach failed -> requeue and duplicate actions.

Commands to reproduce locally (rough):
- Run load generator to simulate burst pattern: functools-based script that sends 200 concurrent requests for 30s, then silence 90s, repeat.
- Observe autoscaler metrics: pool_queue_length, desired_replicas, actual_replicas, node_attach_time

Immediate mitigation ideas (safe):
- Increase autoscaler cooldown in affected pools to 60-120s (trialed - saw improvement).
- Add hysteresis: require X% sustained over Y seconds before scaleDown.
- Temporarily lower preemption aggressiveness for dedicated pools during peak PST window.
- Tag newer instance types for new nodes to avoid NVML attach edge cases.

Follow-ups / to-dos:
- Run controlled A/B for cooldown 60 vs 120 on two canaries (Priya to coordinate traffic split) - JIRA-ENG-4217
- Add debug metrics: node_attach_time_seconds, eviction_reason, pod_move_count_last_5m (instrument serving scheduler)
- Postmortem: collect full timeseries for last 72h around incidents (Miguel)
- Run a chaos run in staging to purposely delay node attach to see cascading behavior.

Notes to self: keep this as a scratch log. When patterns are stable, formalize into runbook entry: "dedicated pool burst resonance" with clear mitigations and config knobs.

Unresolved questions:
- Is there any interaction with new kernel version rolled on 10/29? (ask platform-eng)
- Are older instance types disproportionately affected? Need instance-level attach latency breakdown.

Useful quick links (again):
- canary dashboards: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/dedicated/burst-resonance
- running load generator: github.com/redwood-inference/load-scripts/bursty

End of current snapshot. Will update as experiments proceed.
_notes: private scratchpad - not a runbook yet
